title: Variables, quoting and exit codes
summary: The three things that make bash scripts break: unquoted variables, unchecked failures and word splitting.

steps.title: A script is a file of commands
body: echo "You passed $# args; the first is $1"
You passed 2 args; the first is one
The first line (the **shebang**) says which interpreter runs the file. `$1 $2 ...` are arguments, `$#` their count, `$@` all of them, `$0` the script's name.

steps.prompt: Why does `name = "Ana"` fail with *name: command not found*?
options: With spaces, bash runs a command called `name` with arguments `=` and `Ana`
steps.explain: Assignment is `name=value` with no spaces. Anything else is parsed as a command.

steps.title: Quoting
body: | `'single'` | completely literal: `'$HOME'` is the five characters `$HOME` |
| `"double"` | variables and `$(...)` expand, but the result stays **one word** |
| unquoted `$var` | expands, then is **split on spaces** and **glob-expanded** |
rm $file        # rm gets TWO args: "my" and "report.txt"
rm "$file"      # rm gets one arg: "my report.txt"
Rule for life: **always double-quote variable expansions**: `"$file"`, `"$@"`, `"$(cmd)"`.

steps.explain: Single quotes stop all expansion; double quotes allow it.

steps.prompt: How many lines does this print? (`for` loops over words)
code: for f in $files; do echo "$f"; done
steps.explain: Unquoted `$files` is split on spaces into three words. That's exactly the bug that breaks scripts on filenames with spaces; use arrays (`files=("a b.txt" c)` and `"${files[@]}"`).

steps.title: Exit codes
body: Every command returns an **exit code**: `0` means success, anything else (1-255) means failure. `$?` holds the last one.
echo $?          # 0 if found, 1 if not, 2 if the file is missing
mkdir /srv/app && cd /srv/app      # && runs the right side only on success
cd /nope || echo "cd failed"       # || runs the right side only on failure
Your own scripts should `exit 0` on success and `exit 1` (or another code) on failure, so CI pipelines and other scripts can tell.

steps.prompt: Match the expansion to its meaning.
pairs: exit code of the last command
VAR, or `x` if it's unset or empty

steps.explain: `false && echo A` fails so `|| echo B` runs. `true || ...` skips the right side and leaves `$?` = 0.

steps.prompt: Use the first argument as the environment name, defaulting to `staging`, and fail fast if `cd` doesn't work.
steps.explain: `${1:-staging}` substitutes a default when `$1` is missing. `|| exit 1` stops the script when cd fails, instead of carrying on in the wrong directory.

steps.title: Fix the quoting in a real deploy script
prompt: `~/deploy/deploy.sh FILE [ENV]` copies a build file into `~/sites/ENV/`. It has three bugs a reviewer would catch:
- It is called without ENV most of the time, and should then use `staging`. Today it copies into `~/sites/`.
- `~/build/release notes.txt` has a space in its name, and the script breaks it into two words.
- When the copy fails, it still prints `deployed ...` and exits 0, so the pipeline goes green.
Fix the script (rewrite it with `cat > ~/deploy/deploy.sh <<'EOF'` ... `EOF`, or edit it with `sed -i`) so that it
also passes `shellcheck`, the linter every reviewer runs. Try it: `~/deploy/deploy.sh ~/build/app.js prod`.

checks.name: ENV defaults to staging
checks.fail: `deploy.sh ~/build/app.js` (no ENV) should copy into `~/sites/staging/`. `${2:-staging}` gives a default.

checks.name: a name with spaces works
checks.fail: The file with a space did not arrive in `~/sites/prod/`. Quote every expansion: `cp "$file" "$target/"`.

checks.name: a failed copy fails the script
checks.cmd: rm -rf ~/sites; out=$(~/deploy/deploy.sh ~/build/missing.js 2>&1); rc=$?; echo "exit $rc: $out"; test "$rc" -ne 0 && ! grep -q "^deployed" <<<"$out"
checks.fail: With a missing file, the script should stop with a non-zero exit code and not print `deployed`. `set -euo pipefail` at the top does that.

checks.name: shellcheck is happy
checks.fail: `shellcheck ~/deploy/deploy.sh` still reports problems (below). Each has a code like SC2086 you can look up.

hints: Run `shellcheck ~/deploy/deploy.sh` first: it points at every unquoted `$var` (SC2086).
`env=${2:-staging}` uses `staging` when `$2` is unset or empty. `set -euo pipefail` on line 2 stops the script at the first failing command.

Rewrite it: `cat > ~/deploy/deploy.sh <<'EOF'`, then the lines `#!/bin/bash`, `set -euo pipefail`, `file=$1`, `env=${2:-staging}`, `target="$HOME/sites/$env"`, `mkdir -p "$target"`, `cp -- "$file" "$target/"`, `echo "deployed $file to $env"`, and `EOF`.
solution: # Usage: deploy.sh FILE [ENV]     copies FILE into ~/sites/ENV/ (ENV defaults to staging)
explain: Unquoted `$var` is split on spaces and expanded as a glob, so one odd file name turns `cp` (or worse, `rm`) into a
different command. Quote every expansion unless you want splitting. `--` ends options, so a file named `-rf` is a file.
Put `shellcheck` in CI: it catches these before review does.
